title: Universal representation of NP by \(\omega\)-categorical CSPs
formal:
For every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\), does there exist a countable \(\omega\)-categorical relational structure \(\Gamma\) in a finite relational signature such that
\[L\equiv_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\ ?\]
The relation \(\equiv_T^p\) means deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions in both directions. This reduction convention follows the source’s accompanying non-dichotomy results and the explicit definition in the later monograph; Question 2 itself abbreviates it as polynomial-time equivalence.
why: The question tests whether the symmetry framework that supports infinite-domain algebraic CSP methods is computationally universal for NP under the source’s equivalence convention. A positive answer would place every NP degree into that framework; a negative answer would exhibit a complexity limitation imposed by omega-categoricity itself.
status_note: Question 2 is open in the checked 2008 survey. The accompanying theorem and the January 2026 book postprint establish unrestricted-template universality but not the required omega-categorical Turing equivalence. Bounded primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general representation theorem or refutation; the 2026 scope results concern a narrower template class. This is a limited status check, not exhaustive certification of present openness. The Turing reduction convention is explicitly recovered from the related theorem and later monograph rather than attributed as verbatim wording of Question 2.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: The source poses Question 2 for omega-categorical templates, explicitly distinguishing fixed-template CSP definitions from algorithmic questions requiring presentations.
Bodirsky and Grohe prove arbitrary-template Turing universality and a weaker coNP-with-oracle upper bound when omega-categoricity is imposed.
The monograph, checked in its January 2026 postprint, retains the distinction between arbitrary-template universality and the unresolved NP complexity landscape of omega-categorical templates.

The May revision of Three Fundamental Questions stresses that omega-categoricity alone does not bound CSP complexity, while its new scope reductions concern the narrower finitely bounded homogeneous setting.

importance.reason: This asks whether the main symmetry-based framework for infinite-domain CSP algebra can represent every NP computational problem, clarifying a fundamental boundary beyond finite-template classifications.
importance.basis: Individual reading of Question 2, the exact Turing representation theorem, the weaker omega-categorical oracle upper bound and the later monograph’s reduction convention.

sentences: The question asks whether every NP language is polynomial-time Turing equivalent to a CSP with a fixed omega-categorical template.
Omega-categoricity means that each finite tuple length has only finitely many symmetry orbits, even when the domain is infinite.
The reductions may use adaptive exact membership queries, and no uniform template-construction algorithm or effective template presentation is required.
Universality is known for unrestricted infinite templates, while the known omega-categorical construction gives a weaker oracle upper bound.
A resolution would determine whether this symmetry condition limits computational representation of NP problems.

definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(\Gamma\) has a nonempty finite or countably infinite domain and an interpretation \(R^\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) maps elements of \(I\) to domain values and preserves every positive relation tuple. It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples.

An automorphism of \(\Gamma\) is a bijection of its domain preserving both membership and nonmembership in every relation. It acts on an ordered tuple by applying the same bijection to all coordinates. Two tuples are in the same orbit if some automorphism maps one to the other. The structure is \(\omega\)-categorical here if for every positive integer \(k\), there are only finitely many orbits of ordered \(k\)-tuples. For countably infinite structures in a finite signature, this is equivalent to their complete first-order theory having a unique countably infinite model up to isomorphism. Finite structures are admitted by the same orbit convention. The bound on the number of orbits can depend on \(k\); no fixed global bound, algorithm for orbits, homogeneity or finite list of forbidden patterns is assumed.

A CSP instance is a finite \(\tau\)-structure \(I\) with domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. It is accepted exactly when \(I\to\Gamma\). Repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; duplicate tuples are harmless. The empty structure has the empty homomorphism. Encode \(n\) in unary, then in signature order each relation’s unary list length and its tuples of binary indices, with delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. This defines a total language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) of finite bit strings. The signature and structure are fixed for this language; no infinite table, presentation algorithm or value from \(\Gamma\) is supplied with an instance.

A language lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is witnessed by a certificate of length polynomial in the input bit length and checked by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. A reduction \(K\leq_T^p Q\) is a deterministic oracle Turing machine deciding membership in \(K\) using exact yes/no membership queries to \(Q\). On every input \(x\), all its computation, query writing and answer processing take at most \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed positive constants \(C,d\). Thus query lengths and their number are polynomially bounded. The oracle supplies each membership bit at unit query cost; its own computation is not part of the reduction. Queries may depend on earlier answers, and answers may be negated. No randomness or advice is available.

Polynomial-time Turing equivalence means \(L\leq_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\leq_T^p L\). The two programs and their constants may depend on \(L,\Gamma\), but each works on every finite input. The quantifiers are \(\forall L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists\tau,\Gamma,M_1,M_2,C_1,C_2,d_1,d_2\). No uniform algorithm turning an NP verifier into a template or into these reductions is requested. The source explicitly permits defining a fixed CSP without fixing an effective representation of its infinite template.

This is equivalence of computational problems, not equality of their input classes or their logical definitions. Turing equivalence is also weaker than requiring many-one reductions, which produce one target instance with the same membership answer. No additional hypothesis \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{NP}\) is inserted: Turing equivalence to an NP language alone implies membership in \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\), the class decided by polynomial-time machines with an NP oracle, rather than closure inside NP. The original question does not separately impose that extra condition. Trivial languages are included and cause no difficulty under Turing reductions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every language in NP and produce existence of a finite-signature omega-categorical template with both deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. A negative answer must establish a language in NP for which no permitted template has the required equivalence. Giving an arbitrary infinite template, only one reduction direction, a weaker oracle-complexity upper bound, or a representation for only NP-complete languages does not settle the question. No unproved complexity separation is assumed; conditional constructions or obstructions settle only their conditional statements.

source_formulation.text: Is every problem in NP polynomial-time equivalent to a CSP with an omega-categorical template?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 2; deterministic polynomial-time Turing equivalence is made explicit using the accompanying representation theorem and the author’s later Chapter 13 convention.

context_blocks.text: Infinite templates vastly enlarge the class of possible CSPs, but omega-categoricity retains finitely many symmetry types at each tuple length. It is the structural hypothesis behind many preservation theorems used in algebraic CSP theory. The question asks whether imposing this symmetry still permits representation of every NP computational problem up to the stated reductions.

Bodirsky and Grohe prove that every decision language has a polynomial-time Turing equivalent CSP with an unrestricted infinite template. Their construction is not omega-categorical. Thus arbitrary-template universality is an established starting point, and the symmetry condition is the entire additional issue.

For omega-categorical templates their Theorem 2 instead gives, for any decision language \(L\), a template with \(L\leq_m^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{coNP}^{L}\). Here the first relation is a polynomial-time many-one reduction and \(\mathrm{coNP}^{L}\) means complements of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time machines with exact oracle \(L\). This upper bound does not supply the required deterministic polynomial-time oracle reduction back to \(L\).

The same work constructs omega-categorical templates with coNP-complete CSPs and, conditionally, coNP-intermediate CSPs. These results demonstrate broad complexity within the symmetry class, but they do not establish equivalence to each prescribed NP language. The later book separately retains the question of NP-intermediate omega-categorical CSPs; that question explicitly requires NP membership, unlike bare Turing equivalence.

The stronger restrictions in the Bodirsky–Pinsker dichotomy concern reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. They ensure finite-pattern certificates and hence NP membership. The present target quantifies over all omega-categorical templates and imposes neither restriction; proving that narrower dichotomy would not settle this representation question.

Logical representation is also a different issue. Two templates may define different finite-instance CSPs yet have polynomial-time equivalent decision problems. The source’s neighbouring question about whether a particular SNP-definable CSP has an omega-categorical template asks for the same accepted input class, which is stronger than computational equivalence and has separate counterexamples.
